Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Keanu remembers the smell most vividly. Not the shouting, or the heavy thud of his father’s footsteps on the linoleum, but the acrid scent of cheap, filterless cigarettes and something else—the smell of singed fabric. He had been five, maybe six, small for his age with dark, watchful eyes. The memory arrives not as a story but as a series of sensory explosions. The rough texture of the checked flannel shirt his father always wore, the sudden, sharp heat on his arm, and that burning smell. When it comes back to him now, unbidden, it is accompanied by a white-hot rage that leaves him breathless, his hands clenched so tight his knuckles are white. Something in his surroundings—the pattern on a stranger’s coat, a whiff of smoke from a distant chimney—can instantly bring back the full force of the memory without warning, leaving him disoriented and shaking in the middle of a workday.

For thirty years as a detective, Keanu had managed to compartmentalize. He saw his hypervigilance not as a symptom but as a professional asset. He was the one who noticed the slightly ajar door, the flicker of movement in a dark alley, the subtle lie in a witness’s testimony. He was always on guard, a state that felt as natural and necessary as breathing. At home, this translated into sleeplessness. He would lie awake for hours, certain that he needed to stay alert, listening to the city’s hum, cataloging every siren and distant argument as a potential threat. He had come to believe that the world was a fundamentally unsafe place, and his childhood had simply given him a head start in understanding that truth. His beliefs about fairness and safety had been completely destroyed long before he ever pinned on a badge.

The carefully constructed walls began to crumble a few years ago. His wife left, tired of living with a man who could not tolerate closeness or joy. Any positive emotion—a shared laugh, a moment of peace—felt dangerous to Keanu, a lapse in the constant vigilance that kept him safe. He began to avoid people, first social gatherings, then even casual coffees with colleagues. He felt most secure alone in his apartment, where he could control the environment. He methodically removed anything that could be a reminder, including every checked or flannel shirt he owned, a habit so ingrained he no longer consciously registered the reason for it. When the memories did break through, he learned to detach himself, to watch the scene of the small boy and the angry man play out from a great distance, as if it were a film about someone else.

The current crisis began with a domestic violence case. The victim was a seven-year-old boy who looked hauntingly like his own childhood photos. Standing in the messy living room, taking notes, Keanu was suddenly overwhelmed. The boy’s wide, terrified eyes, the smell of stale smoke in the apartment—it all converged. His heart began to hammer against his ribs, sweat beaded on his forehead, and for a moment, he couldn’t hear what his partner was saying. Later, trying to write the report, the words wouldn't come. When he tried to explain what happened, he would lose the thread and be unable to finish, the narrative fracturing in his mind. The rage he felt on behalf of the child was inseparable from the rage he felt for himself. He was certain his intense physical reaction was proof that he was a lousy coper, that after all these years, he was still weak.

What finally brought Keanu to therapy was the deep, gnawing conviction that the abuse had happened to him because of the sort of person he was—that there was something inherently wrong with him from the start. This belief, which had shadowed his entire life, was now crippling him. He was afraid of losing his job, the one thing that gave his watchfulness a purpose. He sits in the waiting room, not with hope, but with the grim determination of a man cornered, terrified that he is beyond repair but even more terrified of letting the past finally consume him completely.
